title: The Covenant of the One
subtitle: Measure, the Messengers and the Final Account
summary: One Creator beyond every image, a Measure that binds king and beggar alike, Nahira who would not burn incense to the powerful, and a faith with an answer for things that claim to be gods.
content:
> *"Do not make two measures where the One gave one."*
> — Covenant teaching

The **Covenant of the One** is the dominant faith of the [Kharad Compact](factions.html#kharad-compact). It is a strict monotheistic revelation tradition, and it is entirely distinct from the [[faith-of-the-first-light|Faith of the First Light]] shared by Aurelia and Vesper. Where the First Light speaks of Light and its Lantern-Bearers, the Covenant speaks of one Creator, of Measure, of mortal Messengers and of an Account every person must one day give.

The One is known by many titles: **the Most High**, **the First and Last**, **the Keeper of the Final Account**, **the Giver of Measure**, **the Unseen**. The One is beyond physical representation. No image can contain the divine, so Kharadi sacred art avoids depicting it at all, and favours **calligraphy**, **geometry**, **light**, **water** and **celestial motifs** instead.

## Creation and Measure

Everything except the One is created. Nothing else is divine, however powerful it may be. **Power does not equal divinity**: that is one of the Covenant's most important teachings, and, since the Gates opened, one of its most useful.

At the heart of Kharadi faith is the idea of **Measure**. Creation has proper relationships, proportions and balances, and Measure names them all. The same word covers physical quantities, contracts, law, morality and responsibility, and the overlap is deliberate. An honest weight in the market and an honest judgment in court are, to a Kharadi, two expressions of the same thing.

The great principle of Measure is:

> *Do not make two measures where the One gave one.*

It condemns hypocrisy and selective standards. In principle, king and beggar, creditor and debtor, judge and accused are all judged by the same moral rules.

That does not mean circumstances are irrelevant. Kharadi jurists are sophisticated, and they weigh intention, coercion, circumstance and capacity. The principle is that the *rule itself* must not quietly change depending on who stands before it.

### The Same Measure, and Vesper

The **Same Measure** is at the centre of one of the liveliest intellectual arguments in Endros, with the [Vesper Republic](factions.html#vesper-republic). Vesperians object that equal rules can still be unjust when people begin from unequal conditions, and ask the question they ask of everything: *who wrote the principles?* The Kharadi answer is that the principles were **discovered, not invented**, and that circumstances shape how they are applied, never what they are.

It would be wrong to conclude that the Covenant ignores inequality. It takes it very seriously; it simply locates the remedy elsewhere, in mercy, in obligations of wealth and in the way circumstances bear on judgment. And quite often, the two traditions reach the same conclusion by entirely different roads.

> **Two jurists in Endros, on a case of stolen grain**
>
> "I would let her go," said the Vesperian. "She stole to feed her children in a city whose grain contracts were written by the people who sold her the grain. The law that condemns her was never neutral."
>
> "I would also let her go," said the Kharadi. "The law is the same for her as for the grain merchant: taking what is not yours is wrong. But the Measure also weighs coercion, and hunger is coercion. And the merchant who refused her credit while his warehouse was full has his own account to answer for."
>
> The Vesperian considered this. "We agree on the verdict."
>
> "We do."
>
> "That's going to make the dinner very dull."
>
> "On the contrary. Now we can argue about why."

## The Covenant

The Covenant itself is the relationship between the One and humanity. Humanity has been given **reason**, **choice**, **community** and **responsibility**, and is expected to use them.

Power and wealth, in this teaching, are **entrusted**, not earned as a sign of divine favour. A successful merchant cannot say, *I am rich, therefore the One favours me.* Wealth is not proof of anything. It is an additional set of obligations, and a heavier account to give.

## The Messengers

The One has sent **Messengers**: mortal men and women who carried the Covenant's teaching. Messengers are not divine, and they are never to be worshipped. To pray to a Messenger would be to make exactly the mistake the Messengers came to correct.

### Nahira the Witness

The most important Messenger is **Nahira the Witness**. She is remembered for rejecting divine kingship, rejecting the priestly sale of forgiveness, and teaching that every person is morally accountable, whatever their rank.

Her best-known story is the **Night of Broken Idols**.

> **The Night of Broken Idols, as it is recited**
>
> They brought Nahira into the hall where the ruler's ancestors stood in gold, and they put the incense into her hands.
>
> "Honour them," said the ruler. "Every king of my line sits among the gods."
>
> Nahira held the incense and did not move.
>
> "Your ancestors were powerful," she said. "So is a storm. So is a fever. I do not burn incense to them either." She set the incense down on the floor. "I deny that power makes them worthy of worship."
>
> That night the earth shook, and the golden ancestors fell from their places and broke on the floor of the hall.

What the Covenant teaches from this story is not that Nahira caused the earthquake. Commentators have argued for generations about what exactly happened that night, and the Recitation does not settle it. The lesson is what she said: **power does not make something worthy of worship**.

### Qorvan of the Honest Measure

The Covenant also honours a foreign teacher, **Qorvan**, known in translation as **Corven of the Honest Measure**. Kharadi scripture identifies him with the figure the western First Light traditions call **Corven, Keeper of Measures**. The Covenant holds that he was a **mortal Messenger**. The Aurelian [[crowned-sun|Crowned Sun]] honours him as a Lantern-Bearer, a holy figure of a different order altogether. Each side regards the other's reading as a serious error, and the historical relationship between the two Corvens is itself disputed.

His best-known saying is quoted in Kharadi counting-houses and temples alike:

> *A dishonest scale first cheats its owner.*

## The Recitation

The Covenant's scripture is **the Recitation**. Nahira's teachings were first passed on by word of mouth and only later compiled by her followers. The Recitation contains theology, moral teaching, poetry, history, prayer, legal principles and parables.

Kharadi religious life is a life of the text: reading, memorisation, commentary, debate and legal reasoning. A great deal of Kharadi law grew out of arguments about what the Recitation requires, and a great many Kharadi arguments still end with somebody quoting it.

## Law and Faith

The Covenant shapes Kharadi law and commerce more deeply than any other force. Its principles are taught to children and cited in courts:

- **Agreements matter.** A freely made promise creates real responsibility.
- **Fraud corrupts consent.** An agreement obtained by deception is morally compromised, whatever the paper says.
- **Debt is real.** An obligation does not disappear because it has become inconvenient.
- **Mercy is also real.** A debt does not cancel the creditor's duties toward the debtor as a person.
- **Witnesses matter.** Reliable testimony protects both parties.
- **Wealth carries duties.** Owning something never frees you from your obligations.

### The Share of Mercy

The clearest expression of those duties is the **Share of Mercy**, a charitable obligation expected of everyone who can afford it, and especially of the successful. It supports the poor, widows, orphans, travellers, public wells, debtors, hospitals and religious institutions. A Kharadi merchant is expected to contribute to the society that made their success possible. How much is owed, and how it is reckoned, varies by tradition and is not set down here.

> **In the debtors' court at a Kharadi port**
>
> The clerk read out the name, the sum, and the date the debt fell due. The debtor, a ropemaker by the look of his hands, was already standing with his head down.
>
> Before the magistrate could speak, the clerk cleared his throat.
>
> "Your honour, the debt was settled this morning."
>
> The ropemaker looked up. "By whom?"
>
> The clerk checked the receipt. "The payer asked not to be named. The note says only: *from the Share*."
>
> The ropemaker stood there for some time after the court had moved on to the next case.

## The Final Account

After death comes the **Final Account**, when every person's actions and obligations are judged before the One. Kharadis naturally reach for commercial language when they speak of it: accounts, balances, debts and obligations. But no serious teacher describes the afterlife as a literal ledger. The language is a metaphor for **accountability**: for having to answer, fully and honestly, for what you did with what you were given.

## Servants and the Unseen Peoples

The Covenant accepts that the One created spiritual beings as well as physical ones. Some are called **angels**, or **Servants**: powerful, but created, and never divine. Worship belongs only to the One.

Kharadi folklore also knows a different kind of being, often grouped together as **the Unseen Peoples**. They are not angels and they are not automatically evil. They are associated with ruins, wells, crossroads, deserts, storms, abandoned places and strange bargains. Some traditions say they have communities, customs and obligations of their own, and that their dispositions vary as much as anyone's. No single account of them is agreed, and most Kharadis are content to leave it so and simply be polite.

> **At a ruined well on a caravan road**
>
> The young guard watched the old caravan master pour a cup of water onto the stones beside the dry well, and leave the cup there.
>
> "There's nobody here."
>
> "You don't know who else is travelling," said the master, and walked back to the camels.

Many Kharadis keep small customs of this kind, some religious and some simply folk practice. Not everyone believes in all of them:

- do not count your wealth aloud after sunset;
- water given to an unknown traveller is a blessing;
- a sandstorm that begins during a contract negotiation is a bad sign;
- a cracked mirror in a merchant's office is unlucky;
- if your name is called in an empty alley, wait before answering;
- a stone that balances naturally is fortunate;
- receiving exact change may mean no hidden obligation remains;
- feed an unexpected guest before you question them.

## The Covenant and the Gates

The Covenant's answer to the Gates is short: **if it exists, it was created**. Whatever lies beyond a Gate, however strange or powerful, is part of creation and not divine.

That gives Kharadi Expeditioners an unusually firm footing when something beyond a Gate claims to be a god, displays impossible power, or demands worship. Power is not proof of godhood. Nahira said so to a king.

> **A Kharadi chaplain's briefing to a crew before a crossing**
>
> "You may meet things in there that are stronger than you, older than you, and very sure of themselves. Some of them may tell you they are gods. Some of them may be very convincing."
>
> A young surveyor raised her hand. "And if they are?"
>
> "Then they will have no trouble proving it to the One. They do not need to prove it to you." The chaplain looked around the room. "Be polite. Be careful. Do not kneel. Remember Nahira: *a storm is powerful too*.

Two questions remain open. The first is whether some of the beings encountered beyond the Gates belong among the **Unseen Peoples**. Some scholars say yes; others argue that Gate beings need entirely new categories. Nothing is settled.

The second concerns **ownership**. Kharadi teachers have long used a simple analogy: *if you find an unlocked warehouse, its contents do not become yours simply because you can walk in.* The Covenant does not say that taking an artifact, a resource or a Core is theft. It says that **being able to reach something does not prove you own it**. What follows from that for the Gates is one of the most hotly argued questions in Kharadi law and theology today.
